extracted.intended_audience: historians and scholars of Atlantic/imperial history; graduate students in history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and interpreting histories of imperial revolutions in the Atlantic world, urging historians to rethink assumptions about empire, sovereignty, nationhood, and the causes/outcomes of revolutions. The essay reframes methodological priorities and substantive foci for scholarship on empires and their successor polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate studies of imperial crises and origins of nationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring the study of imperial crises together with the study of the origins of nationalism in colonial societies so that each informs the other rather than remaining separate fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question tacit assumptions underpinning both fields; analyze how regimes began to call themselves 'nations' as a result of imperial crises rather than treating nationhood as the automatic successor to empire. Use comparative and transnational perspectives across the Atlantic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teleologies of inevitable imperial decline or national triumph
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume the inevitability of imperial demise or the automatic triumph of nation-states; treat decline and success as contingent outcomes rather than predetermined endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider imperial adaptations and a variety of routes (inversions, backslidings, failed starts) rather than a single progressive narrative from empire to nation. Restore 'might-have-beens' to accounts of the age of revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat revolutions as imperial in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand revolutions as part of empire-wide transformations that yielded new social practices and reworked imperial sovereignty, not merely as secessionist episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how revolutions recast institutional frameworks of imperial sovereignty and produced 'nations' as products of tensions wrought by attempts to reorganize imperial institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center slavery, slave trade, and emancipation in imperial narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the slave trade, slave labor, and struggles for emancipation at the center of accounts of Atlantic empires and revolutions rather than treating them as peripheral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demographic and economic data (e.g., slave importation figures) and studies of slave insurrections (Saint-Domingue/Haiti) to show how slavery shaped imperial crisis and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider sovereignty as plural, contingent, and multi-scalar
rubrics_metrics.description: Recast sovereignty away from a single bounded territorial conception toward a view of sovereignty as a bundle of claims, images, and assertions of authority aggregated at more than one juridical level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize legal pluralism, gray zones, and layered authorities within empires; draw on work showing incomplete territorial contours and the multiplicity of practices that composed imperial rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to legal pluralism and incomplete territorial contours
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that empires combined a variety of institutional practices and possessed incomplete, plural territorial arrangements rather than homogeneous jurisdictional control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples of legal pluralism across colonial contexts (courts, viceregal districts, treaties with indigenous polities) to explain how sovereignty was exercised unevenly across space and populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze reforms and adaptations as central to imperial change
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat administrative, fiscal, and commercial reforms (e.g., Bourbon and Pombaline reforms, mercantilist adjustments) as key mechanisms by which empires sought to reconstitute themselves and that thereby generated resistance and crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine specific reform measures (licensing, fiscal instrumentation, militarization, new legal districts) and how they both strengthened and provoked opposition within metropoles and colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine economic integration and its destabilizing effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how deeper economic integration—expanded Atlantic trade, silver flows, and the trafficking of African captives—both sustained imperial power and created new tensions and dependencies that contributed to crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate economic evidence (trade patterns, mining output, slave trading changes) to show how fiscal pressures and merchant capital shaped imperial strategies and colonial social structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on inter-imperial rivalry and global context
rubrics_metrics.description: Place national revolutions in the broader context of inter-imperial rivalry across the Atlantic and beyond; do not narrate revolutions as isolated, inward-looking national events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative perspectives and global linkages (Seven Years' War, trans-imperial commerce, diplomatic/military competition) to explain how external pressures affected internal imperial dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize the role of total war and international conflict in producing internal crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the wars of the 1790s and the rise of 'total war' as intensifying imperial competition and folding international conflict into civil wars within empires, thereby generating revolutionary conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the French Revolution and Napoleonic conflicts transformed inter-imperial contests into internal struggles over regime form and imperial sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat civil wars within empires as the proximate cause of disintegration and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that civil wars within empires—often sparked or intensified by international war—were the mechanisms that yielded independence, rather than secession as a mature, homegrown option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how internal partisan violence, irregular warfare, and breakdowns in jurisdiction undermined imperial territoriality and produced fragmented post-imperial sovereignties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize empires' resilience and adaptive capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that empires were not simply rigid and doomed; they adapted through administrative, military, and fiscal measures which in many cases prolonged their life or reconstituted authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance narratives of decline with studies of successful reform and reintegration (e.g., British consolidation in India, Iberian recalibrations) to avoid deterministic accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate subaltern actors and social dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the roles and perspectives of subaltern groups—enslaved people, indigenous peoples, plebeians, free blacks—in accounts of imperial crisis and revolutionary change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how mobilization of subaltern actors (e.g., slave soldiers, indigenous uprisings) complicated projects of sovereignty and opened alternative political possibilities that shaped outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject a simple empire-vs-nation dichotomy; allow hybrid and alternative outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reducing outcomes to either 'empire' or 'nation'; recognize hybrid regimes, imperial residuals, restored empires, and varied post-imperial constitutional arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples such as Brazil's imperial monarchy, Mexican empire, and loyalist continuities in Caribbean/Canada to demonstrate the diversity of post-revolutionary political forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace practices and infrastructures of imperial sovereignty on the ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on concrete practices—militias, treaties with borderland peoples, licensing systems, fortifications, and local intermediaries—that constituted imperial authority in specific places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail how such practices created layered sovereignties and negotiated compromises between metropolitan aims and local intermediaries, and how these influenced the course of revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative, transnational, and Atlantic-scale perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt comparative and transnational methods that cross legal, linguistic, and national boundaries to grasp the systemic features of the age of revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthesize case studies from different imperial contexts to reveal shared processes (e.g., fiscal crises, slave trade dynamics, military pressures) and divergences that shaped varied outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret declarations of independence and nation-making as contingent political strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Read declarations of independence and nation-building projects as responses to crises of sovereignty and as strategic attempts to recombine elements of imperial governance, not as inevitable expressions of a nationalist teleology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how elites often sought to preserve aspects of empire (imperial constitutions, monarchical forms) even while repudiating metropolitan rule; analyze rhetoric and institutional continuities alongside ruptures.
